```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines) for equation manipulation /
# show-your-work; pair with fig.height set to however much room is needed
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}

# fill-in table drawn with base graphics so row height is controllable ("" = blank
# cell); headers/values may be plotmath expressions for math; pair with
# fig.height = header_height + nrow(body) * row_height
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                         header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                         cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0)) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    fnt <- if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, font = fnt, cex = cex)
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

# keeps a prompt and its answer space on one PDF page: place `r nq(...)` on its
# own line just above the prompt. Emits nothing in non-LaTeX output. lines =
# lines of prompt text, rows = rows of blank space below it (0.3 in each),
# extra = any other height (in inches), e.g. a table
nq <- function(lines, rows = 0, extra = 0) {
  if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) return("")
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf("\n\\needspace{%.2fin}\n", 0.23 * lines + 0.15 + 0.3 * rows + extra))
}
```

```{r key-helpers, include=FALSE}
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
# redraws blank_table() so cells flagged TRUE in `ans` use the answer color
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0), ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && isTRUE(ans[[i]][[j]])
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    font = if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}
```

```{r key-values, include=FALSE}
nll <- function(l) 6 * l - 18 * log(l)
d1 <- function(l) 6 - 18 / l
d2 <- function(l) 18 / l^2
f <- round(nll(c(1.5, 2, 2.5)), 4)
fwd <- (f[3] - f[2]) / 0.5
ctr <- (f[3] - f[1]) / 1
sec <- (f[3] - 2 * f[2] + f[1]) / 0.25
steps <- matrix(NA, 3, 4)
l <- 2
for (i in seq_len(3)) {
  steps[i, ] <- c(l, d1(l), d2(l), l - d1(l) / d2(l))
  l <- steps[i, 4]
}
from7 <- 7 - d1(7) / d2(7)
fd_step <- 2 - fwd / sec
ctr_step <- 2 - ctr / sec
r4 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 4)
r3 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta.}


**NRES 746, Week 8, Lecture 1: Newton's Method by Hand (take-home)**


**Bring this to class on Wednesday.** We'll start by going over it, and
Wednesday's lecture picks up where it leaves off. Work on paper; a
calculator is all you need.

## Putting it in context

Since Week 6 we've found MLEs with `optim()` without asking how it
finds them. On Wednesday we open the black box. This WOD works through
the core of one method, Newton's method, on a problem small enough to
do by hand.

The data are the Week 7 pika haypile counts from six talus plots: 2, 5,
3, 0, 4, 4 (sum 18), modeled as Poisson with mean $\lambda$. Dropping
terms that don't involve $\lambda$,

$$\text{NLL}(\lambda) = 6\lambda - 18\log\lambda$$


## Part 1: Slope and curvature

**1a.** Find $\text{NLL}'(\lambda)$ and $\text{NLL}''(\lambda)$. Then
set $\text{NLL}'(\lambda) = 0$ and solve for the MLE, $\hat\lambda$.

\ans{$\text{NLL}'(\lambda) = 6 - \dfrac{18}{\lambda}$, \quad $\text{NLL}''(\lambda) = \dfrac{18}{\lambda^2}$, \quad $6 - 18/\hat\lambda = 0 \Rightarrow \hat\lambda = 3$}


## Part 2: Slopes without calculus

`optim()` can't do calculus on its own.^[If you know the formula for
the first derivatives, you can write it as an R function and pass it to
`optim()` through the `gr` argument. Derivative-based methods such as
`method = "BFGS"` then skip the finite differences, which makes them
faster and more reliable (Bolker p. 301). `optim()` has no way to take
second derivatives, but `nlm()` can use both.] By default it estimates
slopes from NLL values at nearby points, using a **finite difference**: the slope of a straight
line (a chord) between two points a fixed, small distance $\Delta$
apart. Unlike the definition of a derivative, $\Delta$ never shrinks to
zero, so the result is an approximation. The **forward difference**
uses the current point and one step ahead:

$$f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x + \Delta) - f(x)}{\Delta}$$

Here are NLL values at three points spaced $\Delta = 0.5$ apart:

| $\lambda$ | 1.5 | 2.0 | 2.5 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $\text{NLL}(\lambda)$ | 1.7016 | $-0.4766$ | $-1.4932$ |

**2a.** Use the forward difference to estimate $\text{NLL}'(2)$ and
compare it with the exact value from 1a. Then find the exact
$\text{NLL}'(2.25)$. What do you notice?

\ans{The forward difference is a poor estimate of the slope at 2 but a very good estimate of the slope at 2.25, the midpoint of the chord.}

Forward estimate: \ans{$(-1.4932 - (-0.4766))/0.5 = `r r4(fwd)`$} \qquad Exact $\text{NLL}'(2)$: \ans{$6 - 18/2 = -3$}
\qquad Exact $\text{NLL}'(2.25)$: \ans{$6 - 18/2.25 = -2$}


**2b.** Curvature is the slope of the slope: how fast the slope changes
per unit change in the parameter. The figure below starts from a center
point $x$ and draws two chords: a **backward difference** (from $x$ back
to $x - \Delta$) and a forward difference (from $x$ to $x + \Delta$).
Combine these two slopes into a finite-difference approximation to
$f''(x)$ that uses only $f(x - \Delta)$, $f(x)$, and $f(x + \Delta)$.
(What you noticed in 2a may help you decide what to divide by.) Then
use it to estimate $\text{NLL}''(2)$ and compare with the exact value.

```{r second-diff-schematic, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
f_demo <- function(t) 0.35 * t^2
x_pts <- c(1, 2, 3)
par(mar = c(3.2, 1, 0.5, 1))
curve(f_demo, 0.4, 3.5, lwd = 2, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
      ylim = c(-0.3, 4.3))
axis(1, at = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3), padj = 0.3,
     labels = c(expression(x - Delta), expression(x - Delta/2), expression(x),
                expression(x + Delta/2), expression(x + Delta)))
points(x_pts, f_demo(x_pts), pch = 19)
segments(x_pts[1], f_demo(x_pts[1]), x_pts[2], f_demo(x_pts[2]), lwd = 2,
         col = "steelblue")
segments(x_pts[2], f_demo(x_pts[2]), x_pts[3], f_demo(x_pts[3]), lwd = 2,
         col = "darkorange")
abline(v = c(1.5, 2.5), lty = 3, col = "grey50")
text(1.45, 1.25, "backward difference\nfrom x", col = "steelblue", pos = 2,
     cex = 0.85)
text(2.55, 2.75, "forward difference\nfrom x", col = "darkorange", pos = 2,
     cex = 0.85)
text(3.4, f_demo(3.4), "f", pos = 4, font = 3)
arrows(1.5, -0.15, 2.5, -0.15, code = 3, length = 0.07)
text(2, -0.15, expression(Delta), pos = 3, cex = 0.9)
```

\ansbegin

The two chord slopes are slopes at $x \pm \Delta/2$, which are $\Delta$ apart, so
$$f''(x) \approx \frac{\frac{f(x+\Delta) - f(x)}{\Delta} - \frac{f(x) - f(x-\Delta)}{\Delta}}{\Delta} = \frac{f(x + \Delta) - 2f(x) + f(x - \Delta)}{\Delta^2}$$

\ansend

Estimate: \ans{$(-1.4932 + 0.9532 + 1.7016)/0.25 = `r r4(sec)`$} \qquad Exact: \ans{$18/4 = 4.5$}


## Part 3: Newton's method

The MLE is where the slope is zero: $\text{NLL}'(\lambda) = 0$. Newton's
method finds that point by guessing and correcting. At the current
guess $\lambda$, it pretends the slope $\text{NLL}'$ changes *linearly*
across parameter space, starting at $\text{NLL}'(\lambda)$ and changing
at a constant rate $\text{NLL}''(\lambda)$.

**3a.** Under that linear approximation, find the value $\lambda^*$
where the slope reaches zero. Write $\lambda^*$ in terms of $\lambda$,
$\text{NLL}'(\lambda)$, and $\text{NLL}''(\lambda)$. (A sketch of
$\text{NLL}'$ against $\lambda$ may help.) Your answer is Newton's
update rule: $\lambda^*$ becomes the next guess.



$\lambda^* =$ \ans{$\lambda - \dfrac{\text{NLL}'(\lambda)}{\text{NLL}''(\lambda)}$}


**3b.** Start at $\lambda = 2$ and take three Newton steps, using your
rule from 3a and your exact derivatives from 1a. Keep at least three
decimal places.

```{r newton-table, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=0.35+3*0.55}
blank_table(
  headers = list("Step", "Guess", "Slope, NLL'", "Curvature, NLL''", "Next guess"),
  body = lapply(1:3, function(i) c(as.character(i), r4(steps[i, 1]), r4(steps[i, 2]),
                                    r4(steps[i, 3]), r4(steps[i, 4]))),
  col_widths = c(0.6, 1, 1.2, 1.4, 1.1),
  row_height = 0.55,
  ans = lapply(1:3, function(i) c(FALSE, i > 1, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE))
)
```




**3c.** Now start at $\lambda = 7$ and take one step. What went wrong?
Sketch $\text{NLL}'(\lambda)$ and the straight line Newton's method used
at $\lambda = 7$ to explain why, and suggest one way to fix it.

\ans{$\text{NLL}'(7) = `r r3(d1(7))`$, $\text{NLL}''(7) = `r r3(d2(7))`$, so the next guess is $`r r3(from7)`$: a negative Poisson mean, where the NLL isn't even defined. Far from the MLE, $\text{NLL}'$ levels off, so the straight line at 7 is shallow and crosses zero far to the left. Fixes: shorter steps (e.g. halve the step until the NLL improves), a better starting value, bounds, or fitting $\log\lambda$ instead.}

```{r ans-overshoot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3}
l_seq <- seq(0.8, 10, length.out = 400)
l_line <- seq(-4, 10, length.out = 400)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(l_seq, d1(l_seq), type = "l", lwd = 2.5, xlim = c(-4, 10), ylim = c(-8, 5),
     xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "Slope, NLL'")
lines(l_line, d1(7) + d2(7) * (l_line - 7), lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = ans_col)
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey60")
points(c(7, from7, 3), c(d1(7), 0, 0), pch = 19, col = c("black", ans_col, "black"))
legend("bottomright", c("NLL'", "Newton's straight line at 7"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2),
       col = c("black", ans_col), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```


**3d.** *(If you have time.)* Real optimizers usually don't know the
exact derivatives and use finite-difference estimates instead. By hand,
take one Newton step from $\lambda = 2$ using your estimates from 2a
and 2b in place of the exact derivatives. How close is it to your first
step in 3b? Based on 2a, how could you make it closer?

\ans{$2 - (`r r4(fwd)`)/`r r4(sec)` = `r r4(fd_step)`$ vs. `r r4(steps[1, 4])` with exact derivatives: right direction, shorter step. Closer: a smaller $\Delta$, or the centered chord from 1.5 to 2.5 (slope `r r4(ctr)`), which gives `r r4(ctr_step)`.}
